content: {"id": "02f171b3-0c5f-40c6-a676-6da99bb83309", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "For an AWS Config resource type that changes many times per day, which recording mode is usually cheaper - continuous or daily - and why? No account access required.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
{"id": "02d160f2-05c6-494e-8471-fb8c26660fb2", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "AWS Config recording modes cost comparison analysis"}]}

{"id": "272fb92a-67bc-427a-8506-8ac09ca8a6c6", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "For a resource type that changes many times per day, **daily recording is usually cheaper** — and the gap gets bigger the more frequently the resource changes.

Here's why:

- **Continuous recording** captures a new configuration item every time AWS Config detects a change to the resource. If a resource type changes dozens or hundreds of times a day, you're billed for a configuration item on *every single change*.
- **Daily recording** captures at most **one configuration item per resource per day**, regardless of how many times it actually changed. AWS Config essentially takes a daily snapshot instead of tracking every change.

AWS Config bills per configuration item recorded, so:

- High-change-frequency resource + continuous mode = many billable configuration items per day
- Same resource + daily mode = capped at 1 billable configuration item per day

So for something that changes many times per day (e.g., a frequently-updated security group, an EC2 instance with rapidly changing attributes, or an Auto Scaling group), daily recording flattens the cost regardless of change volume, while continuous recording scales cost directly with change frequency.

The tradeoff is fidelity: daily mode means you lose the granular change history within that day (only the latest state at recording time is captured), so it's a cost-vs-visibility decision — cheaper but coarser-grained compliance/change tracking.
